The first release published to nuget.org, and a fix for a packaging defect that shipped silently in both releases before it.

```sh
dotnet add package IbkrDotNet.Extensions.DependencyInjection --prerelease
```

No API changes. The public surface is byte-for-byte what `v0.2.0` transcribed — still 90 of IBKR's 108 Trading endpoints.

## Fixed: Source Link never worked

`v0.1.0` and `v0.2.0` were packed with no commit recorded. The `.nupkg` carried a `<repository>` element with a URL and nothing else, and the `.snupkg` carried a PDB with no source URLs at all, so a debugger could not step into the source of either package.

The cause was one line:

```xml
<GlobalPackageReference Include="Microsoft.SourceLink.GitHub" Version="10.0.400" />
```

The .NET SDK has carried Source Link in-box since .NET 8. Referencing the package explicitly does not reinforce that, it **replaces** it — and the standalone package does not enable the source-control queries the SDK's own copy turns on. Nothing about the failure is visible from a build: packages pack, tests pass, `dotnet nuget push` succeeds, and the omission surfaces only when somebody attaches a debugger months later.

Removing the reference restores both halves. This release records `branch` and `commit` in both packages, and `PackagingTests` now fails the build if the reference comes back or if `PublishRepositoryUrl` is dropped. The release workflow re-checks the packed nuspec against the commit it is building before it pushes anything, because the guard that matters is the one nearest the irreversible step.

Nothing can be done about the two releases already published. Their artifacts remain attached to their GitHub releases; neither was ever on nuget.org.

## Why this is a prerelease

Two reasons, and neither is doubt about the client.

The release pipeline had never run against nuget.org — no version of this package has ever been pushed, and the workflow that pushes it is not exercised by CI, since it only runs on a tag. This tag is that pipeline's first real test. A prerelease number is the cheap one to spend on it.

The second is the API itself. `0.x` already means the public surface can change, and the two Financial Advisor groups are still unimplemented. `--prerelease` makes that an explicit opt-in rather than something a consumer discovers from the version number.

`0.3.0` proper follows once this has proven the path end to end.

## Publishing

Pushed by [Trusted Publishing](https://learn.microsoft.com/nuget/nuget-org/trusted-publishing) over OIDC, so there is no long-lived nuget.org API key in this repository's secrets. The workflow packs, verifies the commit is recorded, publishes the GitHub Release, requests a credential valid for one hour, pushes the core package before the one that depends on it, and then reads the public feed to confirm both versions are actually live — a green push exit code is not evidence of that, because nuget.org validates asynchronously.

## Not in this release

WebSocket streaming remains out of scope. The remaining 18 endpoints are the two Financial Advisor groups, tracked as [#21](https://github.com/jerbersoft/ibkrdotnet/issues/21) and [#22](https://github.com/jerbersoft/ibkrdotnet/issues/22). `IIbkrApiClient` reaches them today with authentication, rate limiting and error mapping intact.
